assessment.nobel_worthiness: Collateral constraints, credit cycles and the amplification of shocks form a foundational framework in macro-finance. It shapes how economists model financial frictions, asset prices and crises, and it has had durable influence on theory and policy analysis. The contribution is conceptually clear and general.
assessment.attribution: The core mechanism is the Kiyotaki-Moore credit-cycles model, so the credit for it is concentrated in two people. Gertler and Gilchrist are important on the financial accelerator and empirical implementation, but that strand overlaps with the earlier Bernanke recognition, so the two-person selection is cleaner.
assessment.maturity: The central work dates from the 1990s, and its relevance was reinforced by the 2008 crisis and later research. It has had ample time for scrutiny and consolidation.
uncertainties: The committee may see macro-finance as already covered by the 2022 banking-crisis prize.
Attribution between the credit-cycle strand and the financial-accelerator strand could be contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data have changed what is empirically known about intergenerational mobility, neighbourhood effects and equality of opportunity. The designs are transparent, the data large, and the results have had substantial policy and academic reach. Credible, reproducible empirical work of this kind meets common criteria well.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the central figure across the mobility program, and Hendren is closely tied to the neighbourhood-effects work. Friedman and Katz are significant co-contributors, so cutting the list to two leaves out collaborators who did substantial work. Because this is a large team program, credit allocation is difficult.
assessment.maturity: The main papers date from roughly 2014 onward. Impact is already large, but the program is still being extended and some long-horizon findings and causal interpretations are still being tested.
uncertainties: Some neighbourhood-effect and mobility-measurement results may still be revised in follow-up work.
Some committee members may judge the program too recent.
The boundary of credited contributors is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Melitz model of heterogeneous firms and selection into exporting reorganised trade theory and empirics. It linked firm-level data to aggregate gains from trade, and Helpman's related work on firm heterogeneity and the organisation of trade extended it. The influence on research and policy analysis is very broad.
assessment.attribution: Melitz is clearly central, and Helpman is a major architect of the wider new-new trade agenda. Redding is a strong contributor to quantitative extensions, but he is not part of the core origin. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not on this credited list despite their related empirical contributions.
assessment.maturity: The foundational paper is from 2003, with more than two decades of confirmation and extension. The framework has been tested heavily, and some quantitative implications have been refined or qualified.
uncertainties: The 2008 trade prize may reduce the committee's appetite for another trade award.
Attribution relative to related firm-level contributors outside the credited names is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Formalising and testing social preferences (reciprocity, fairness, inequity aversion, costly punishment) changed how economists model motives and cooperation. The experimental results have replicated reasonably well in large-scale replication efforts, and the ideas have spread to contract theory, labour and public economics.
assessment.attribution: Fehr is the most prominent figure for both the experimental evidence and the theory (with Schmidt). Falk contributed substantially to field and representative-sample evidence on preferences. Rabin, Bolton and Ockenfels are related contributors who are not credited here. Parts of the credit already sit with earlier behavioural and experimental prizes.
assessment.maturity: The key papers are from 1999 onward and have been tested extensively. Open debates concern the stability and context dependence of the preferences, but the core findings are well supported.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2002 and 2017 behavioural prizes and the 2019 experimental-approach prize.
The model-versus-evidence balance between the theory and the experimental work is uncertain.
My own research is close to this area, so I flag it as a possible source of bias.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Task-based accounts of technology and the local labour-market effects of import competition changed the understanding of wage inequality, polarisation and adjustment costs. The work has had large academic and policy influence. The China-shock design is empirically clear.
assessment.attribution: The China-shock results are tied to Autor, Dorn and Hanson. The task-based framework also draws on Acemoglu, Katz and others, so credit for the broader technology-and-inequality theme is spread across several scholars.
assessment.maturity: The China-shock papers are from around 2013 and have been repeatedly re-examined. The adjustment-cost conclusions are widely accepted, though magnitudes and the role of automation remain debated.
uncertainties: Debate continues over effect sizes and identification in the shift-share designs.
Credit for the task-based framework overlaps with scholars who are not credited or who have already been recognised.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: A systematic framework linking electoral rules, constitutions and fiscal policy established modern political economics, with both theory and empirical tests. The influence on the field is deep and lasting.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini jointly produced the central synthesis and the empirical constitutional-effects program. Besley is also important for state capacity and political agency, but the core of the framework is the Persson-Tabellini partnership.
assessment.maturity: The central work dates from the 1990s and 2000s. It is widely absorbed in the literature, though some empirical cross-country findings have been questioned.
uncertainties: The 2024 institutions prize may reduce the committee's appetite for a political-economy award.
Persson's role in the committee's past may create a sensitivity, and I treat it as unresolved.
Some cross-country empirical results are open to identification objections.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Uncertainty shocks and policy-uncertainty measurement created a large literature on how uncertainty affects investment, hiring and the business cycle. The text-based policy-uncertainty index is widely used, and the work is empirically and methodologically influential.
assessment.attribution: Bloom is central to the theoretical and micro-level uncertainty-shock work, and Davis to the uncertainty-and-reallocation tradition and the index with Baker and Bloom. Baker is a major contributor, but a three- to four-person set would dilute attribution.
assessment.maturity: The key papers are from 2009 and 2016. Policy-uncertainty measures are well adopted, but the causal macro effects are still contested, so the work is less settled than the older candidates.
uncertainties: It is hard to separate the causal effect of uncertainty from first-moment shocks.
The index's reliance on newspaper text may raise measurement concerns.
Maturity is lower than for the older candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Historical and tax-record series on top incomes reopened distributional measurement and made inequality central to economic debate. The influence on the field and on public discussion is very large.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez built the top-income series and the long-run framework together. Zucman is important for offshore wealth and distributional national accounts, but his work is more recent. Atkinson, a major pioneer, has died and is not credited.
assessment.maturity: The foundational series date from the early 2000s, and the program continues. Measurement choices for wealth and capital-share claims remain disputed, which weighs against it.
uncertainties: Methodological critiques of the wealth-concentration and capital-share conclusions are unresolved.
Some of the theoretical framing is more contested than the measurement contributions.
Public prominence may overstate scientific consensus.
